title: Fire at Mabila
place: Mabila (exact site uncertain), central Alabama, USA
text: Chief Tascaluza, an elaborately plumed leader of the Mabila, refused Hernando de Soto's demand for bearers and was held hostage. On the morning of October 18, 1540, Soto's troops reached Mabila, the palisaded capital. A quarrel between a Spanish officer and a townsman turned violent, and in the melee the Spaniards set fire to the town, burning it and many of its people.

source.name: Encyclopedia of Alabama: European Exploration and Colonial Period

title: A French Fort Built with Timucua Help
text: On June 30, 1564, French colonists under Laudonnière began building Fort de la Caroline in today's Florida. They chose the spot partly for their ties with the Timucua-speaking Mocama people, who they hoped would provide food, since the French never seriously tried farming. The local leader Saturiwa sent 80 men to help raise the triangular fort of earth, wood and turf.

source.name: National Park Service, Timucuan Ecological and Historic Preserve: Settlement and Conflict

title: The White Lion at Point Comfort
place: Old Point Comfort, Hampton, Virginia, USA
text: On August 25, 1619, the privateer ship White Lion reached Old Point Comfort in Virginia carrying enslaved Africans from the kingdom of Ndongo, in present-day Angola. English privateers had seized them from the Spanish slave ship São João Bautista in the Gulf of Mexico. At Point Comfort, 15 women and 17 men were traded to English colonists for food.

source.name: National Park Service: Arrival of the First Africans in 1619

title: The Colonies' First Printed Book
text: The Bay Psalm Book, printed in Cambridge in 1640, was the first book printed in British North America. Its press had belonged to Reverend Jose Glover, who died crossing the Atlantic; his widow Elizabeth set it up at Harvard College. Running it fell to their indentured servant Stephen Daye, a locksmith. Perhaps 1,700 copies were printed, and only 11 survive.

source.name: New York Public Library: New in Digital Collections: The Bay Psalm Book

title: Jeanne Mance and Ville-Marie
text: Jeanne Mance landed at Quebec in August 1641 and was part of the small group that founded Ville-Marie, the future Montreal, on 17 May 1642. That autumn she opened the Hôtel-Dieu, its hospital. In the desperate year of 1651 she offered the governor, Maisonneuve, 22,000 livres given to her hospital so he could fetch help, and her advice saved Montreal.

source.name: Dictionary of Canadian Biography: Mance, Jeanne

title: The Quake That Buried Trees
place: Charlevoix, between Baie-Saint-Paul and La Malbaie, Quebec, Canada
text: In 1663 an earthquake of about magnitude 7.5, the largest ever to hit eastern North America, shook what is now Quebec. Its epicentre was probably between Baie-Saint-Paul and La Malbaie, and it set off huge landslides, some more than 300 kilometres away, that buried whole trees. Geological Survey of Canada researchers radiocarbon-date those trunks to learn how often such quakes strike.

source.name: Natural Resources Canada: Why are researchers interested in an earthquake that occurred over 300 years ago?

title: Canoes onto the Mississippi
place: Mouth of the Wisconsin River, near Prairie du Chien, Wisconsin, USA
text: In mid-May 1673, Louis Jolliet and Father Marquette set out from Michilimackinac by canoe, following Green Bay and the Fox River, then portaging to the Wisconsin. In June, after a journey of more than 500 miles, their canoes entered the Mississippi. They went far enough south to be certain it emptied into the Gulf of Mexico, then turned back, fearing capture by the Spaniards.

source.name: Dictionary of Canadian Biography: Jolliet, Louis

title: Tekakwitha Becomes Catherine
place: Gandaouagué, Mohawk Valley, New York, USA
text: Tekakwitha, daughter of a Kanyen'kehà:ka (Mohawk) father and an Algonquin mother, survived the smallpox that killed her parents when she was four, though it scarred her and weakened her eyes. At Easter 1676, aged 20, she was baptized Catherine. Persecuted at home, she later travelled several hundred kilometres to the mission at Kahnawà:ke. In 2012 she became the first Indigenous woman in North America made a saint.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Saint Kateri Tekakwitha

title: The Rat's Last Speech
text: Kondiaronk, a Wendat chief from Michilimackinac whom the French called Le Rat, persuaded Indigenous nations to gather at Montreal for the Great Peace of 1701. Over 700 allied people arrived in 200 canoes. Though sick with fever, he spoke for nearly two hours about his peacemaking. He died the next day and was buried in Notre-Dame church: Here lies the Rat, Huron Chief.

source.name: Dictionary of Canadian Biography: Kondiaronk

title: Freedom at Fort Mosé
place: Fort Mose, St. Augustine, Florida, USA
text: Enslaved Africans in the Carolina Colony learned they could escape their British masters and find freedom in Spanish Florida if they became Catholic and pledged to serve the Spanish Crown. In 1738 Governor Manuel de Montiano gave them land about two miles north of St. Augustine. Led by Francisco Menendez, Fort Mosé held thirty-eight men and their families, about one hundred people.

source.name: National Park Service, Fort Matanzas: Fort Mose

title: Calling Out Liberty at Stono
text: On September 9, 1739, enslaved men near South Carolina's Stono River took guns and powder from a warehouse and set off toward Spanish Florida, which had promised freedom. A letter from that year says they grew from twenty to above sixty, marching with colours displayed and two drums beating, calling out Liberty. The militia routed them the next day; perhaps a hundred people died.

source.name: Charleston County Public Library, Charleston Time Machine: The Stono Rebellion of 1739: Where Did It Begin?

title: A Naturalist's Hurried Day in Alaska
text: On July 20, 1741, men from Vitus Bering's ship St. Peter went ashore on Kayak Island for water. The naturalist Steller hurried down the beach and found a still smouldering fire, scraps of fish and a cellar stocked with fish, signs of Alaska Natives who stayed unseen. He described the plants until told to come aboard immediately or be left behind.

source.name: National Park Service: Bering Expedition Landing Site

title: Indigo and Enslaved Labour
text: With her father called back to Antigua, the young Eliza Lucas managed her family's plantations and the enslaved workers on them. She was determined to perfect growing indigo, a dye plant, around Charleston, and in 1744 she grew enough to begin making dye. Built on the exploitation of enslaved workers, the trade boomed: in 1747, 138,300 pounds of dye were exported to England.

source.name: National Park Service, Charles Pinckney National Historic Site: Eliza Lucas Pinckney

title: A Key on a Kite String
text: In June 1752, while waiting for Philadelphia's Christ Church steeple to be finished, Benjamin Franklin decided a kite could reach the storm clouds just as well. He attached a metal key, and his 21-year-old son William was the only witness. When the key showed signs of electrical charge, Franklin knew lightning was a form of electricity, and championed pointed lightning rods.

source.name: The Franklin Institute: Franklin's Lightning Rod

title: Acadians Forced from Grand-Pré
text: Acadian families at Grand-Pré had built dykes to drain salt marsh into rich farmland. In 1755 New England officer John Winslow took charge of deporting them, and some 2,200 Acadian men, women and children were sent away from Les Mines, about a third of the nearly 6,000 deported from Nova Scotia that year. Longfellow later set his poem Evangeline here.

source.name: Parks Canada: History of Grand-Pré National Historic Site

title: Pontiac Moves on Detroit
text: After the British commander Amherst ended the custom of giving presents and limited trade to the forts, Pontiac, war chief of the Ottawas at Detroit, called secret councils from 27 April 1763, stirred partly by the prophet Neolin. On 7 May he entered the fort with some 300 men, but Gladwin had doubled the guard. From 26 May, other forts across the region fell.

source.name: Dictionary of Canadian Biography: Pontiac

title: The Kumeyaay Strike Back
place: Mission San Diego de Alcalá, San Diego, California, USA
text: The Kumeyaay were angry that Spanish missionaries took land, destroyed food-gathering places and harmed Native women and children. Village headmen and doctors planned an attack, and fifteen of twenty-five nearby rancherias sent warriors. Around one o'clock on the night of November 5, 1775, more than six hundred people surrounded Mission San Diego, set it on fire and killed three people, including Father Luis Jayme.

source.name: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian, Native Knowledge 360: The 1775 Kumeyaay Revolt and Destruction of Mission San Diego

title: Yuquot, Already Ancient
place: Yuquot (Friendly Cove), Nootka Island, British Columbia, Canada
text: When Captain James Cook reached Nootka Sound in March 1778, Yuquot was already ancient. The Mowachaht had lived there for over 4,300 years; it was the capital for 17 tribes of the region and the origin of Nuu-chah-nulth whaling. Soon its harbour became a hub of the sea otter trade, and Spain held its only garrison in present-day Canada here.

source.name: Parks Canada, Directory of Federal Heritage Designations: Yuquot National Historic Site of Canada

title: Mum Bett Sues for Freedom
text: Enslaved in Colonel Ashley's house, Mum Bett overheard men discussing a bill of rights saying all people were born free and equal. Lawyer Theodore Sedgwick took her case, and on August 22, 1781, a Great Barrington jury ruled she was not Ashley's property, awarding her and Brom 30 shillings each. She took the name Elizabeth Freeman and later bought her own house.

source.name: National Constitution Center: Elizabeth Freeman, her case for freedom and the Massachusetts Constitution

title: Awa'uq, the Refuge Rock
place: Awa'uq, off Sitkalidak Island, Kodiak archipelago, Alaska, USA
text: On August 14, 1784, Russian fur trader Grigorii Shelikhov attacked several thousand Alutiiq people sheltering on a refuge rock, a small steep-walled island off Sitkalidak Island. After a standoff, his men crossed a spit exposed at low tide and fired cannon and muskets; estimates of the dead range from 200 to 500. The place is still called Awa'uq, meaning to become numb.

source.name: Alutiiq Museum and Archaeological Repository: Alutiiq Museum Launches Refuge Rock Monument Planning Project (press release, August 12, 2026)

title: The River That Ran the Wrong Way
place: Mackenzie River delta, Northwest Territories, Canada
text: Fur trader Alexander Mackenzie left Fort Chipewyan on 3 June 1789, searching for a water passage across the continent to the Pacific. His party included a Chipewyan man known as English Chief. But the great river ran north, not west. Mackenzie pushed on to the sea anyway, spent four nights on Whale Island, and was back at the fort after 102 days.

source.name: Dictionary of Canadian Biography: Mackenzie, Sir Alexander

title: Chloe Cooley's Scream
text: On 14 March 1793, Adam Vrooman tied up Chloe Cooley, the Black woman he enslaved, and forced her into a boat to sell her across the Niagara River into New York. She resisted fiercely. Her scream alerted Peter Martin, a Black Loyalist, who reported it to the government. That July, Upper Canada passed the first law in a British colony restricting the slave trade.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Chloe Cooley
